lessons.title: Atoms, Elements, Compounds and the Model of the Atom

before.content_html:
What are Atoms?

Everything around us is made up of tiny particles called atoms. Atoms are incredibly small — about 0.1 nanometres across. To put this in perspective, if an atom was the size of a football, a football would be the size of Earth!

Key Fact

All substances are made of atoms. Atoms cannot be created or destroyed in chemical reactions.

Atoms are made up of three types of particles: protons, neutrons, and electrons. Understanding how these particles are arranged helps us understand how different elements behave and react with each other.

Elements and the Periodic Table

An element is a pure substance that contains only one type of atom. For example, oxygen contains only oxygen atoms, and carbon contains only carbon atoms. There are about 100 different elements, and they’re all organised in the periodic table.

Each element has a unique atomic number. This tells us how many protons are in each atom of that element. Hydrogen has atomic number 1 (1 proton), helium has atomic number 2 (2 protons), and so on.

Elements in the same column (group) of the periodic table have similar properties because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell. This affects how they react with other elements.

Compounds and Chemical Formulas

When atoms of different elements join together, they form compounds. For example, water (\(H_2O\)) is a compound made from hydrogen and oxygen atoms. The chemical formula tells us exactly which atoms are present and in what ratio.

Key Fact

In chemical formulas, the small numbers (subscripts) tell us how many atoms of each element are present. \(H_2O\) means 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.

Common compounds you should know include:

  • Water: \(H_2O\) (hydrogen and oxygen)
  • Carbon dioxide: \(CO_2\) (carbon and oxygen)
  • Sodium chloride: \(NaCl\) (sodium and chlorine)
  • Methane: \(CH_4\) (carbon and hydrogen)

The Structure of the Atom

Modern atomic theory tells us that atoms have a specific structure. At the centre is the nucleus, which contains protons and neutrons. Around the nucleus, electrons move in regions called electron shells or energy levels.

Protons: Positively charged particles in the nucleus. The number of protons determines what element the atom is.

Neutrons: Neutral particles (no charge) in the nucleus. They add mass to the atom but don’t affect its chemical properties.

Electrons: Negatively charged particles that move around the nucleus in shells. They’re involved in chemical bonding.

The relative masses are important to remember: protons and neutrons each have a relative mass of 1, while electrons have a relative mass of almost zero (about 1 over 1836 to be precise).

How the Atomic Model Developed

Our understanding of atomic structure has changed dramatically over time as scientists gathered new evidence. This shows how scientific knowledge develops through experimentation and discovery.

1803

Dalton’s Atomic Theory

John Dalton proposed that all matter was made of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms. He thought atoms were like tiny solid spheres.

1897

Discovery of the Electron

J.J. Thomson discovered electrons and proposed the ‘plum pudding’ model — atoms were positive spheres with negative electrons embedded in them.

1909

Rutherford’s Gold Foil Experiment

Ernest Rutherford fired alpha particles at gold foil. Most passed through, but some bounced back, proving atoms have a tiny, dense nucleus.

1913

Bohr’s Model

Niels Bohr proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus in specific energy levels or shells, like planets around the sun.

Each new discovery built on previous work and led to a better understanding of atomic structure. This is a great example of how scientific knowledge is provisional — it can change when new evidence is discovered.

Mass Number and Atomic Number

Every element can be described using two important numbers. The atomic number tells us how many protons are in the nucleus. The mass number tells us the total number of protons and neutrons.

We can use these numbers to work out the number of each type of particle in an atom:

  • Number of protons = atomic number
  • Number of neutrons = mass number - atomic number
  • Number of electrons = number of protons (in a neutral atom)
Key Fact

In a neutral atom, the number of protons always equals the number of electrons. This means the positive and negative charges balance out.

Key Takeaways

  • All matter is made of atoms, which contain protons, neutrons, and electrons arranged with a nucleus at the centre
  • Elements contain only one type of atom, while compounds contain atoms of different elements chemically bonded together
  • Our model of atomic structure has evolved over time as scientists made new discoveries and gathered evidence

lessons.title: The Periodic Table and Its Groups

before.content_html:
The Development of the Periodic Table

Before the discovery of protons and neutrons, scientists attempted to classify elements by arranging them in order of atomic weight. Dmitri Mendeleev (1869) arranged elements in order of atomic weight but left gaps for undiscovered elements and swapped some elements so that those with similar properties lined up in the same columns. When elements such as gallium and germanium were later discovered and matched his predictions, his table was widely accepted.

The modern periodic table arranges elements in order of atomic number (not atomic weight). Elements in the same group (column) have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, giving them similar chemical properties. Elements in the same period (row) have the same number of electron shells.

Key Fact

Elements are arranged by atomic number. Groups (columns) share the same number of outer electrons and similar properties. Periods (rows) share the same number of electron shells. Metals are on the left; non-metals are on the right.

Group 1 — Alkali Metals

The alkali metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) all have one electron in their outer shell. They are soft, have low density and react vigorously with water, producing a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas:

$$2Na + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + H_2$$

Going down Group 1, reactivity increases because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and is more easily lost (less electrostatic attraction). The elements also have lower melting points and higher densities going down the group.

Group 7 — Halogens

The halogens (F, Cl, Br, I, At) have seven electrons in their outer shell. They exist as diatomic molecules (\(Cl_2\), \(Br_2\), etc.) and react with metals to form ionic compounds called halides (e.g. NaCl).

Going down Group 7, reactivity decreases because the outer shell is further from the nucleus, making it harder to gain an extra electron. A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from its compound, e.g. chlorine displaces bromine from potassium bromide.

Key Fact

Group 1: reactivity increases down the group (easier to lose outer electron). Group 7: reactivity decreases down the group (harder to gain an electron). These trends are opposite because metals lose electrons while non-metals gain them.

The noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn) have full outer electron shells, making them very stable and unreactive. They are used where inert gases are needed: helium in balloons and airships, neon in advertising signs, argon in light bulbs and welding. Boiling point increases down the group.

Transition metals are found in the central block of the periodic table. They have typical metallic properties: high melting points, high density, good conductors. Unlike Group 1 metals, transition metals are less reactive, harder and denser. They form coloured compounds and can act as catalysts (e.g. iron in the Haber process).

lessons.title: Quantitative Chemistry: Mass, Moles and Concentrations

before.content_html:
What Are Moles?

A mole is the unit chemists use to count atoms, molecules and ions. Just like a dozen equals 12 items, one mole equals 6.02 × 10²³ particles. This huge number is called Avogadro's constant.

Key Fact

One mole of any element has a mass in grams equal to its relative atomic mass. For example, one mole of carbon (relative atomic mass 12) has a mass of 12g.

The molar mass connects the microscopic world of atoms to the macroscopic world we can measure. For compounds, we add up the relative atomic masses of all atoms present.

Calculating Moles from Mass

The fundamental equation linking moles, mass and molar mass is:

\(\text{number of moles} = \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{molar mass}}\)

This can be rearranged to find mass or molar mass depending on what information you're given.

Calculate the number of moles in 44g of carbon dioxide (CO₂).

Step 1: Find the molar mass of CO₂

Carbon: 1 × 12 = 12g/mol

Oxygen: 2 × 16 = 32g/mol

Total molar mass = 12 + 32 = 44g/mol

Step 2: Apply the formula

\(\text{moles} = \frac{44}{44} = 1 \text{ mole}\)

Concentration of Solutions

When substances dissolve in water, we create solutions. The concentration tells us how much solute is dissolved in a given volume of solution.

Key Fact

Concentration can be measured in g/dm³ (mass concentration) or mol/dm³ (molar concentration). Both are essential for different types of calculations.

The two main concentration equations you need to know are:

$$\text{concentration (g/dm³)} = \frac{\text{mass of solute (g)}}{\text{volume of solution (dm³)}}$$

\(\text{concentration (mol/dm³)} = \frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{volume of solution (dm³)}}\)

Remember these volume conversions:

  • 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³ = 1000 ml = 1 litre
  • To convert cm³ to dm³: divide by 1000
  • To convert dm³ to cm³: multiply by 1000

Calculating Masses in Reactions

Chemical equations show the molar ratios between reactants and products. We can use these ratios along with molar masses to calculate the masses of substances involved in reactions.

The process follows these steps:

  1. Write the balanced chemical equation
  2. Identify the molar ratio from the equation
  3. Calculate moles of the known substance
  4. Use the molar ratio to find moles of unknown substance
  5. Convert moles back to mass using molar mass

Calculate the mass of water produced when 16g of methane burns completely.

\(CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O\)

Step 1: Calculate moles of methane

Molar mass of CH₄ = 12 + (4 × 1) = 16 g/mol

\(\text{moles of CH}_4 = \frac{16}{16} = 1 \text{ mole}\)

Step 2: Use molar ratio

From equation: 1 mole CH₄ produces 2 moles H₂O

Therefore: moles of H₂O = 1 × 2 = 2 moles

Step 3: Convert to mass

Molar mass of H₂O = (2 × 1) + 16 = 18 g/mol

\(\text{mass of H}_2\text{O} = 2 × 18 = 36\text{g}\)

Limiting Reactants

In many reactions, one reactant runs out before the others. This limiting reactant determines how much product can be formed.

To identify the limiting reactant, calculate how many moles of each reactant you have, then compare this to the molar ratios in the balanced equation. The reactant that would be used up first is the limiting reactant.

Common Calculation Mistakes

Students often make errors when working with quantitative chemistry. Always check your balanced equations are correct before starting calculations. Make sure you convert units properly — especially converting cm³ to dm³ for concentration calculations. Remember that molar mass uses the relative atomic mass from the periodic table, and for compounds you must add up all the atoms present.

lessons.title: Reactivity of Metals and Metal Extraction

before.content_html:
The Reactivity Series

Metals can be arranged in order of their reactivity — this is called the reactivity series. The most reactive metals (potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium) react vigorously with water and acids. Less reactive metals (zinc, iron, copper, silver, gold) react more slowly or not at all.

A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from its compound. For example, if iron is placed in copper sulfate solution, the iron displaces the copper:

$$Fe + CuSO_4 \rightarrow FeSO_4 + Cu$$

Key Fact

The reactivity series (most to least reactive): K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, C, Zn, Fe, H, Cu, Ag, Au. Carbon and hydrogen are included as reference points. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound.

Extraction of Metals

Metals are found in the Earth’s crust, often combined with other elements in ores. The method of extraction depends on the metal’s position in the reactivity series:

  • Metals less reactive than carbon (e.g. iron, copper, zinc) are extracted by reduction with carbon. Carbon is cheaper and more reactive, so it removes the oxygen from the metal oxide.
  • Metals more reactive than carbon (e.g. aluminium, sodium, potassium) must be extracted by electrolysis, which is more expensive because it requires large amounts of electricity.

For example, iron is extracted from iron oxide using carbon in a blast furnace:

$$2Fe_2O_3 + 3C \rightarrow 4Fe + 3CO_2$$

Oxidation is the gain of oxygen (or loss of electrons). Reduction is the loss of oxygen (or gain of electrons). Remember: OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain. In a displacement reaction, the more reactive metal is oxidised (loses electrons) and the less reactive metal ion is reduced (gains electrons).

Key Fact

Metals below carbon in the reactivity series are extracted by reduction with carbon. Metals above carbon need electrolysis. Oxidation = gain of oxygen / loss of electrons. Reduction = loss of oxygen / gain of electrons.

Recycling metals saves energy (less needed than extraction from ore), reduces the use of limited ore resources, reduces waste going to landfill, and reduces environmental damage from mining and carbon emissions. However, collection and sorting can be difficult, and recycled metals may be impure.

lessons.title: Reactions of Acids, pH and Neutralisation

before.content_html:
Acids, Bases and the pH Scale

An acid is a substance that produces hydrogen ions (\(H^+\)) when dissolved in water. A base is a substance that can neutralise an acid. An alkali is a soluble base that produces hydroxide ions (\(OH^-\)) in water.

The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. Acids have a pH below 7, neutral solutions have a pH of 7, and alkalis have a pH above 7. pH can be measured with universal indicator or a pH probe.

Key Fact

Acids produce \(H^+\) ions in water; alkalis produce \(OH^-\) ions. The pH scale: 0–6 = acidic, 7 = neutral, 8–14 = alkaline. Neutralisation: \(H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O\).

Neutralisation Reactions

Neutralisation occurs when an acid reacts with a base. The ionic equation is:

$$H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O$$

The key reactions of acids are:

  • Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen. E.g. \(Mg + 2HCl \rightarrow MgCl_2 + H_2\)
  • Acid + metal oxide → salt + water. E.g. \(CuO + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow CuSO_4 + H_2O\)
  • Acid + metal hydroxide → salt + water. E.g. \(NaOH + HCl \rightarrow NaCl + H_2O\)
  • Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. E.g. \(CaCO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2\)

The salt produced depends on which acid is used: hydrochloric acid (\(HCl\)) makes chlorides, sulfuric acid (\(H_2SO_4\)) makes sulfates, and nitric acid (\(HNO_3\)) makes nitrates.

To make a pure, dry salt: add an excess of insoluble base or metal oxide to the acid, filter off the excess solid, then evaporate the water from the filtrate to leave salt crystals. This is Required Practical 1.

Key Fact

HCl → chlorides. \(H_2SO_4\) → sulfates. \(HNO_3\) → nitrates. To predict the salt name: metal name + acid type (e.g. magnesium + sulfuric acid = magnesium sulfate).

Strong acids (e.g. hydrochloric, sulfuric, nitric acid) fully ionise in water — every acid molecule releases its \(H^+\) ions. Weak acids (e.g. ethanoic acid, citric acid) only partially ionise — an equilibrium is established between ionised and un-ionised molecules. At the same concentration, a strong acid has a lower pH than a weak acid.

What Is Electrolysis?

Electrolysis is the process of using electricity to break down an ionic compound into its elements. The compound being broken down is called the electrolyte and must be either molten or dissolved in water so that the ions are free to move.

The electrolyte is placed between two electrodes: the cathode (negative electrode) attracts positive metal ions, and the anode (positive electrode) attracts negative non-metal ions.

Key Fact

Electrolysis: positive ions (cations) move to the cathode (negative electrode), negative ions (anions) move to the anode (positive electrode). At the cathode, metals are deposited. At the anode, non-metals are released.

At the cathode, positive metal ions gain electrons (reduction) to form metal atoms. At the anode, negative ions lose electrons (oxidation) to form atoms or molecules. Remember: PANIC — Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.

Electrolysis of Molten Compounds

When a molten binary ionic compound (e.g. lead bromide, \(PbBr_2\)) is electrolysed:

  • Cathode: \(Pb^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Pb\) (lead metal is deposited — reduction).
  • Anode: \(2Br^- \rightarrow Br_2 + 2e^-\) (bromine gas is released — oxidation).

When an ionic compound is dissolved in water, there are additional \(H^+\) and \(OH^-\) ions from the water. The rules for predicting products at each electrode are:

Cathode: If the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, hydrogen gas is produced. If less reactive than hydrogen, the metal is deposited.

Anode: If a halide ion is present, the halogen is produced. If no halide is present, oxygen is produced (from \(OH^-\) ions).

Extraction of Aluminium

Aluminium is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon, so it is extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide (\(Al_2O_3\)). The aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite to lower the melting point and reduce energy costs.

At the cathode: \(Al^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow Al\) (aluminium is deposited).

At the anode: \(2O^{2-} \rightarrow O_2 + 4e^-\) (oxygen is released). The carbon anodes gradually burn away because the oxygen reacts with them at high temperature, so they need regular replacement.

Key Fact

Aluminium extraction: electrolysis of \(Al_2O_3\) dissolved in cryolite. Al deposited at cathode, \(O_2\) at anode. Carbon anodes burn away and need replacing. The process uses large amounts of electricity, making it expensive.

Required Practical 4 involves electrolysing aqueous solutions using inert (carbon or platinum) electrodes. You observe the products at each electrode and test them: hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop, chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper, and oxygen relights a glowing splint.

before.description: Properties of transition metals and the unique characteristics of nanoparticles.
before.content_html:
Transition Metals

The transition metals are found in the central block of the periodic table, between groups 2 and 3. They include everyday metals like iron, copper, nickel, and gold. Compared with Group 1 metals (alkali metals), transition metals have very different physical and chemical properties.

Key Fact

Transition metals have higher melting points, are harder and stronger, and are much denser than Group 1 metals. They are also less reactive and do not react as vigorously with water or oxygen.

Key properties of transition metals that distinguish them from Group 1 metals:

  • High melting points — iron melts at 1538 °C compared to sodium at just 98 °C.
  • High density — this makes them useful as structural materials (e.g. iron in construction).
  • Good conductors of heat and electricity (e.g. copper is used in electrical wiring).
  • Form coloured compounds — many transition metal compounds have distinctive colours: copper sulfate is blue, iron(III) oxide is orange-brown, potassium permanganate is purple.
  • Act as catalysts — iron is the catalyst in the Haber process; manganese dioxide catalyses the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.

Group 1 metals (lithium, sodium, potassium) are soft, have low melting points, low density, and are very reactive — they react vigorously with water. Transition metals are the opposite: hard, high melting points, high density, and much less reactive. This is why transition metals are used for structural and electrical applications, while Group 1 metals are not.

Transition metals can also form ions with different charges (e.g. iron can form Fe²+ and Fe³+), which is why they form compounds with different colours.

Nanoparticles

Nanoparticles are extremely small particles with at least one dimension between 1 and 100 nanometres (nm). A nanometre is one billionth of a metre: \(1\text{ nm} = 1 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m}\).

Key Fact

Nanoparticles have a very high surface area to volume ratio compared with bulk materials of the same substance. This gives them different properties, including different colours, higher reactivity, and different electrical conductivity.

As particles get smaller, their surface area to volume ratio increases dramatically. To illustrate: a single 1 cm cube has a surface area of 6 cm². If you cut it into 1 mm cubes, the total surface area increases to 60 cm² — ten times more surface for the same volume of material.

Uses of Nanoparticles

Because of their unique properties, nanoparticles have many applications:

  • Medicine: Silver nanoparticles have antibacterial properties and are used in wound dressings and some deodorants.
  • Sunscreens: Titanium dioxide nanoparticles provide UV protection without the thick white appearance of traditional sunscreen.
  • Electronics: Nanoparticles are used in computer chips and sensors to create smaller, more efficient components.
  • Catalysis: The high surface area means nanoparticle catalysts are more effective, requiring less material.

Nanoparticles are a relatively new technology, and there are concerns about their safety:

  • They are so small that they can enter cells and even cross the blood-brain barrier, with unknown long-term health effects.
  • The long-term environmental impact of releasing nanoparticles into water and soil is not fully understood.
  • Their high reactivity could cause unexpected chemical reactions inside the body.

More research is needed before nanoparticles can be declared completely safe for widespread use.

Key Fact

Nanoparticles can be compared in size to other structures: atoms are about 0.1 nm, nanoparticles are 1–100 nm, fine particles (PM 2.5) are 100–2500 nm, and coarse particles (dust) are 2500–10,000 nm.

lessons.title: Yield, Atom Economy, Molar Concentrations and Gas Volumes

before.description: Calculating percentage yield, atom economy, concentration in mol/dm³, and gas volumes.
before.content_html:
Percentage Yield

In any chemical reaction, the amount of product actually made is often less than the theoretical maximum. The percentage yield compares what you actually get with what you theoretically could get:

$$\text{Percentage yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100$$

Reasons why the yield is less than 100%:

  • The reaction may be reversible — not all reactants convert to products because the reaction reaches equilibrium.
  • Product may be lost during transfer between containers, or during filtration, evaporation, or other separation steps.
  • Side reactions may produce unwanted by-products instead of the desired product.
Key Fact

A high percentage yield is desirable in industrial chemistry because it means less waste, lower costs, and more efficient use of raw materials. A yield of 100% is rarely achievable in practice.

Atom Economy

Atom economy measures how efficiently a reaction uses its starting materials. It compares the mass of the desired product with the total mass of all products:

$$\text{Atom economy} = \frac{M_r \text{ of desired product}}{\text{Total } M_r \text{ of all products}} \times 100$$

Consider the reaction: \(\text{CaCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_2\)

If the desired product is calcium oxide (CaO), \(M_r\) of CaO = 56, \(M_r\) of CO2 = 44.

Total \(M_r\) of all products = 56 + 44 = 100.

$$\text{Atom economy} = \frac{56}{100} \times 100 = 56\%$$

This means 44% of the mass of the reactants ends up as the unwanted by-product (carbon dioxide).

Key Fact

High atom economy is important for sustainability. Reactions with low atom economy produce more waste by-products. Addition reactions have 100% atom economy because all atoms end up in the single product. Substitution and elimination reactions have lower atom economy because they produce by-products.

Molar Concentrations

The concentration of a solution can be expressed in mol/dm³ (moles per cubic decimetre). This tells you how many moles of solute are dissolved in each dm³ of solution.

The key formula is:

$$\text{concentration (mol/dm}^3\text{)} = \frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{volume of solution (dm}^3\text{)}}$$

Remember that 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³ = 1 litre. To convert cm³ to dm³, divide by 1000.

Example: 0.5 mol of NaCl is dissolved in 250 cm³ of water. Calculate the concentration.

Volume = 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.25 dm³

$$\text{Concentration} = \frac{0.5}{0.25} = 2.0 \text{ mol/dm}^3$$

Gas Volumes and the Molar Volume

At room temperature and pressure (RTP: 20 °C, 1 atmosphere), one mole of any gas occupies the same volume: 24 dm³ (or 24,000 cm³). This is called the molar volume.

Key Fact

To calculate the volume of a gas at RTP: $$\text{Volume (dm}^3\text{)} = \text{moles} \times 24$$ To calculate moles from volume: $$\text{Moles} = \frac{\text{volume (dm}^3\text{)}}{24}$$

Example: Calculate the volume of 0.3 mol of carbon dioxide at RTP.

$$\text{Volume} = 0.3 \times 24 = 7.2 \text{ dm}^3$$

lessons.title: Titrations, Chemical Cells and Fuel Cells

before.description: How to carry out titrations accurately, and how chemical and fuel cells generate electricity.
before.content_html:
Titrations

A titration is a practical technique used to find the precise volume of an acid or alkali needed to neutralise a known volume of the other. It is a required practical for AQA Separate Chemistry and a very commonly tested topic.

Key Fact

In a titration, the solution in the burette is added to the solution in the conical flask until the indicator shows the end point — the exact point at which neutralisation is complete.

Titration Method

  1. Use a pipette to measure an exact volume of alkali (e.g. 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide) into a conical flask.
  2. Add a few drops of indicator (e.g. phenolphthalein or methyl orange).
  3. Fill a burette with the acid solution and record the starting volume.
  4. Slowly add acid from the burette to the flask, swirling continuously.
  5. Near the end point, add the acid drop by drop until the indicator permanently changes colour.
  6. Record the final burette reading. The volume of acid used = final reading − initial reading.
  7. Repeat the titration until you have concordant results (two or more results within 0.10 cm³ of each other). Calculate a mean from the concordant results only, ignoring any anomalous results.

Once you have the titre (volume of acid used), you can calculate the unknown concentration:

Step 1: Calculate moles of the known solution: \(\text{moles} = \text{concentration} \times \text{volume (dm}^3\text{)}\)

Step 2: Use the balanced equation to find the mole ratio and calculate moles of the unknown.

Step 3: Calculate the unknown concentration: \(\text{concentration} = \frac{\text{moles}}{\text{volume (dm}^3\text{)}}\)

Example: 25.0 cm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³ NaOH was neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of HCl.

Moles of NaOH = 0.10 × 0.025 = 0.0025 mol

From \(\text{NaOH} + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\), the ratio is 1:1, so moles of HCl = 0.0025 mol.

Concentration of HCl = 0.0025 ÷ 0.020 = 0.125 mol/dm³

Chemical Cells (Batteries)

A chemical cell (battery) produces electricity from chemical reactions. When two different metals are placed in an electrolyte (a conducting solution), a voltage is produced because the metals have different reactivities.

Key Fact

The voltage produced by a chemical cell depends on the difference in reactivity between the two metals. The greater the difference in reactivity, the higher the voltage. For example, zinc and copper produce a higher voltage than iron and copper because zinc is more reactive than iron.

In a chemical cell, the more reactive metal is oxidised (loses electrons) at the negative electrode, and the less reactive metal (or its ions) is reduced (gains electrons) at the positive electrode. Electrons flow through the external circuit from the more reactive to the less reactive metal.

Non-rechargeable cells: The chemical reactions are irreversible. Once the reactants are used up, the cell can no longer produce electricity and must be disposed of.

Rechargeable cells: The chemical reactions are reversible. Passing an electrical current through the cell reverses the reactions, regenerating the original reactants. Examples include lithium-ion batteries used in phones and laptops.

Fuel Cells

A fuel cell produces electricity from the reaction of a fuel (usually hydrogen) with oxygen. Unlike batteries, fuel cells do not run out — they produce electricity continuously as long as fuel and oxygen are supplied.

Key Fact

In a hydrogen fuel cell, the overall reaction is: \(2\text{H}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\). The only waste product is water, making fuel cells a clean energy source. At the negative electrode: \(\text{H}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}^+ + 2e^-\) (oxidation). At the positive electrode: \(\text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ + 4e^- \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\) (reduction).

Advantages of hydrogen fuel cells: the only waste is water (no carbon dioxide), they are very efficient, and they can power vehicles. Disadvantages: hydrogen is difficult and expensive to store and transport, most hydrogen is currently produced from fossil fuels, and fuel cell technology is expensive.
